scope_note: A sourced comparison of speech-enhancement and echo-cancellation tools -- "why does my demo sound bad on a laptop mic, and what fixes it before the rest of the pipeline ever sees the audio." Covers pure noise-suppression models, echo-cancellation libraries, and commercial suites that bundle both. This project runs no PESQ/STOI/SI-SDR benchmarks of its own; quality figures are attributed and marked accordingly.
method_note: Every claim is checked against the vendor's own documentation or source repository before publication, then adversarially audited in a second pass that actively tries to refute each field rather than confirm it, followed by a dedicated facet-recheck pass verifying every facet against the row's own (possibly-corrected) text. Quality/latency figures are mostly vendor-reported and marked verification: vendor-claim or mixed unless independently confirmed.

systems.name: RNNoise
systems.price_note: Free, open source (self-hosted / embedded in your own build)
systems.method: Hybrid DSP + small recurrent neural network (GRU, 215 units across 4 hidden layers, ~87,500 weights): classic pitch/spectral-band features feed the RNN, which requires ~175,000 FLOPS/frame (17.5 Mflops for real-time use) to predict per-band suppression gains; total algorithm complexity including FFTs and pitch search is ~40 Mflops for real-time processing. Described in Valin's 2018 paper 'A Hybrid DSP/Deep Learning Approach to Real-Time Full-Band Speech Enhancement.'
systems.availability: C source library (BSD-3-Clause) at github.com/xiph/rnnoise; WASM builds, LADSPA/PulseAudio plugins, and browser integrations (e.g. Jitsi's rnnoise-wasm) are third-party wrappers around the same core library.
systems.best_for: Squeezing usable real-time noise suppression onto CPU-constrained or embedded voice paths (VoIP clients, phone-class or embedded CPUs) where a full deep-filtering model is too heavy.
systems.watch: The repo does not publish a PESQ/STOI table for the shipped model. The model has continued to be retrained past the original 2018 paper -- most recently a Jan 2025 update ('Augmentation/loss tuning, adding more noise data') on top of 2024 changes that added a VAD output and skip connections -- so there is no published benchmark showing what those retrainings actually improved. On modern full-band content or multi-talker babble it is generally expected to trail newer full-band models like DeepFilterNet, though no controlled head-to-head against the current weights is published.
systems.standout: Small enough to run inside a few hundred kFLOPs/frame on a phone-class CPU core, which is what got it embedded directly inside dozens of VoIP clients and browser calling stacks rather than left as an offline processing step.
systems.quality_note: The original 2018 paper (arXiv:1709.08243) reports PESQ MOS-LQO gains over SpeexDSP's MMSE suppressor across babble/car/street noise via graphed curves, not a summary number, and the repo does not publish an updated PESQ/STOI table for the current (2025-retrained) model. An independent third-party paper (RNNoise-Ex, arXiv:2105.11813, 2021) evaluated its own retrained reference copy of RNNoise on the Edinburgh/Valentini-Botinhao noisy-speech test set (built from two VCTK speakers) and reports PESQ-WB and STOI as bar charts by noise type and SNR level; no single aggregate PESQ figure is stated anywhere in that paper's text, so a precise number cannot be verified against the source. That paper's 'reference' RNNoise was also its own retrain rather than the officially shipped weights, and predates the 2024-2025 architecture/data updates.
systems.latency_note: Processes 10 ms frames; designed for hard real-time use with negligible added algorithmic delay beyond the frame size.
systems.adoption: Embedded inside numerous VoIP/communication clients (e.g. Mumble, various WebRTC-based apps) and packaged as WASM by projects such as Jitsi; no aggregate install or usage figures are published by the project itself.
systems.released: 2017 initial release; hybrid DSP/RNN approach described in the 2018 paper
systems.verification_note: License, availability, and architecture are confirmed from the primary GitHub repo and the original 2018 paper; the paper's own FLOPS figures were checked and an earlier draft's method figure corrected to match. A claim that the shipped model dates to a 2017-2018 training dataset was checked against the repo's own commit history and found false -- the model was last retrained in January 2025. A previously-cited 'PESQ-WB ≈ 2.29' figure could not be located in the cited third-party paper's text (results there are presented only as bar charts) and has been removed as unverifiable.

systems.name: DeepFilterNet
systems.method: Two-stage 'deep filtering' network operating on log-power spectral features: a first stage predicts a coarse spectral envelope, a second stage applies a small complex-valued deep filter that refines periodic (voiced) speech components, per the DeepFilterNet2/3 papers (Schröter et al.).
systems.availability: Rust core with a Python (PyPI) wrapper and training/eval tooling; ships a real-time LADSPA/PipeWire plugin for live microphone noise suppression on Linux, plus pre-compiled binaries for Linux/macOS/Windows.
systems.best_for: Full-band (48 kHz) real-time noise suppression on an ordinary laptop or desktop CPU where you want materially better quality than RNNoise without needing a GPU.
systems.watch: The headline PESQ (~3.17) and STOI (~0.944) figures for DeepFilterNet3 are the authors' own benchmark numbers from their Interspeech 2023 paper, not an independently audited head-to-head comparison against competitors under identical test conditions. Separately, treat this as community-sustained rather than actively developed: the last merged commit was September 2024 and the last tagged release (v0.5.6) was August 2023; several community PRs (WASM SIMD perf work, torch-version compatibility) have sat unmerged since early-to-mid 2026, and recent issues are being closed by a stale-issue bot or by the reporters themselves rather than the maintainer. There is also an open, unanswered GitHub issue (#697, filed 2026-07-15, with a lone non-maintainer comment on 2026-07-27) asking whether the MIT/Apache-2.0 grant covers the pretrained model weights or only the source code — worth resolving before relying on the weights commercially.
systems.standout: Reaches state-of-the-art-level full-band quality at roughly 0.19x real-time factor on a single CPU thread — no GPU required for inference, unlike most models that clear a comparable perceptual-quality bar.
systems.quality_note: DeepFilterNet3 self-reports PESQ 3.17, CSIG 4.34, CBAK 3.61, COVL 3.77, and STOI 0.944 in the Interspeech 2023 paper ('DeepFilterNet: Perceptually Motivated Real-Time Speech Enhancement'); these are the authors' own benchmark on their own test set, not an independent replication.
systems.latency_note: ~0.19x real-time factor on a single laptop CPU thread (DeepFilterNet3), with roughly 40 ms of added algorithmic latency (20 ms window + 10 ms hop + two-frame lookahead) per the DeepFilterNet2 paper; a --compensate-delay flag is provided to account for STFT/ISTFT delay.
systems.adoption: Used as the noise-suppression backend inside at least one third-party Android wrapper (KaleyraVideo/AndroidDeepFilterNet); the project itself does not publish aggregate usage figures.
systems.verification_note: License, method, hardware requirements, and RTF are confirmed from the primary repo and papers. The PESQ/STOI/CSIG/CBAK/COVL figures are the authors' self-reported benchmark, not independently verified here.

systems.name: Facebook Denoiser (Demucs-based)
systems.price_note: Free for non-commercial / research use only under CC BY-NC 4.0; no commercial licensing path is published.
systems.method: Causal waveform-domain encoder-decoder with skip connections, adapted from the Demucs music source-separation architecture, trained end-to-end with combined time-domain and multi-resolution STFT losses (Interspeech 2020 paper, Défossez et al., 'Real Time Speech Enhancement in the Waveform Domain,' arXiv:2006.12847).
systems.availability: Python/PyTorch library (pip-installable); GitHub repo (facebookresearch/denoiser) has been archived and made read-only by the owner since October 31, 2023.
systems.best_for: A research reference / baseline for waveform-domain (not spectral-mask) speech enhancement — not a fit for a production commercial product given the non-commercial licence and archived, unmaintained state.
systems.watch: Licence-catch: CC BY-NC 4.0 blocks commercial use outright with no published paid tier, and the repository has been archived (read-only, no further commits) since October 31, 2023, so bugs, dependency breaks, and compatibility issues will not be fixed going forward.
systems.standout: One of the few well-known denoisers that operates directly on the raw waveform rather than a spectral mask, jointly trained with an L1 waveform loss and a multi-resolution STFT loss, and the paper's own claim is that it 'matches state-of-the-art performance of both causal and non-causal methods' while doing so.
systems.quality_note: The Interspeech 2020 paper reports PESQ/STOI results on the Valentini benchmark and states the model 'matches state-of-the-art performance of both causal and non-causal methods,' but the abstract does not surface the exact figures and the GitHub README publishes only CPU real-time-factor benchmarks, not quality scores.
systems.latency_note: Author-reported real-time factor on a quad-core 2 GHz Intel i5 laptop CPU: the H=48 model runs at 0.8 RTF single-threaded / 0.6 RTF on 4 threads; the larger H=64 model runs at 1.2 RTF single-threaded / 1.0 RTF on 4 threads (RTF < 1.0 means faster than real time).
systems.verification_note: License, archive status, and method are directly confirmed from the primary GitHub repo, its LICENSE file, and the paper. No unverifiable vendor quality claims are asserted beyond the paper's own qualitative 'matches SOTA' language, which is quoted rather than treated as a number.

systems.name: NVIDIA Maxine Audio Effects (AFX) SDK
systems.licence: Wrapper/sample code on GitHub: MIT. Actual DNN models/binaries: separate NVIDIA SDK licence agreement (free download, gated behind NVIDIA Developer Program / NGC registration)
systems.price_note: Free SDK/model download, gated behind NVIDIA Developer Program (NGC) registration; no published per-minute or per-seat fee — the real cost is the required NVIDIA Tensor Core GPU.
systems.method: GPU-accelerated (Tensor Core, CUDA/TensorRT) deep-learning denoising, dereverberation ('Room Echo Removal'), and a dedicated Acoustic Echo Cancellation effect for near-end mic echo; ships as a Windows SDK for client-side integration and a Linux SDK for server/datacenter deployment (named support for Tesla T4/V100 and Ampere A2-A100-class Tensor Core GPUs; Ada/Hopper support varies by effect and SDK build), processing 32-bit float audio at 16kHz or 48kHz. The underlying model architecture is not published by NVIDIA.
systems.availability: Free SDK download via NVIDIA Developer Program/NGC; MIT-licensed API/sample-code wrapper on GitHub (NVIDIA-Maxine/Maxine-AFX-SDK), proprietary DNN models/binaries via a separate NVIDIA-hosted installer; the noise-removal and room-echo-removal effects also ship inside the free consumer NVIDIA Broadcast app (GeForce RTX 2060+ required).
systems.best_for: Studio, broadcast, or datacenter conferencing pipelines — or an on-prem inference box — that already has a spare NVIDIA Tensor Core GPU and wants GPU-accelerated denoise + dereverb + AEC ahead of ASR, instead of fitting a model inside a CPU compute budget. Not usable for a GPU-less laptop-mic demo.
systems.watch: No CPU fallback, no AMD/Apple Silicon path, and no single latency figure — NVIDIA publishes per-GPU real-time throughput tables (batches/second), not millisecond numbers. The Acoustic Echo Cancellation effect is labelled BETA in NVIDIA's own docs. Ada/Hopper GPUs are not yet supported on the Linux SDK (named support tops out at A100-class). The GitHub wrapper is MIT, but the functional models/DLLs remain proprietary under NVIDIA's own SDK licence — 'open source' claims about this SDK need to be scoped to the wrapper only. The free consumer NVIDIA Broadcast app's RTX-2060 minimum is specific to Broadcast — it does not apply to the server-side Linux SDK, which targets named datacenter Tensor Core GPUs instead.
systems.standout: GPU (Tensor Core) accelerated dereverberation is a first-class, separately-selectable 'Room Echo Removal' effect — paired with acoustic echo cancellation and noise removal in one SDK — rather than folded silently into a generic denoiser, letting it run heavier neural models in real time than a CPU compute budget (e.g. RNNoise, DeepFilterNet) allows.
systems.quality_note: No PESQ/STOI/SI-SDR figures published in the SDK user guide, programming guide, or NVIDIA technical blog for any of the three effects (noise removal, AEC, Room Echo Removal).
systems.latency_note: No single-stream millisecond or real-time-factor latency figure is published. NVIDIA instead publishes per-GPU-architecture real-time throughput tables (batches supported in real time), e.g. AEC: 1,664 batches (16kHz)/576 (48kHz) on a T4, up to 5,700/3,072 on an A100; Room Echo Removal 16kHz: T4 3,240, A10 6,600, A100 17,020, L40 14,440, H100 19,340.
systems.adoption: Noise removal has been bundled inside the free NVIDIA Broadcast app since 2020; Room Echo Removal was added in Broadcast v1.2 (May 2021). NVIDIA's own blog confirms OBS Studio 28.0 has 'native integration of the AI-powered NVIDIA Broadcast virtual background and room echo removal effects.' Other third-party integrations (vMix, AVerMedia, Notch) were checked and could not be confirmed for these specific audio effects, so are not asserted here.
systems.released: RTX Voice beta April 2020; NVIDIA Broadcast app launched September 2020; Audio Effects SDK v1.0 documented since April 2021; current GitHub release v1.3.0 (June 2026)
systems.verification_note: GPU/OS support, throughput numbers, BETA status, and licensing structure all come from NVIDIA's own SDK docs, GitHub repo/LICENSE, and product pages; no independent PESQ/STOI or single-stream latency benchmark was found. This row consolidates one SDK that a research pass independently discovered three times under three names/categories (noise-suppression, echo-cancellation, commercial-suite) into a single entry — see `gaps`.

systems.name: Krisp
systems.licence: Proprietary — commercial licence required to embed the SDK; consumer app sold under subscription
systems.price_note: Meeting-assistant app from $8-15/user/mo (Core $16/mo or $8/mo billed annually; Advanced $30/mo or $15/mo annually; Enterprise custom-priced), following a 7-day free trial of full premium features (unlimited noise cancellation, no credit card required). As of Aug 2026 there is no permanent free tier — a previously-advertised '60 min/day free' tier is no longer on the live pricing page. The developer Voice SDK is a separate, sales-approved commercial licence with no public price list.
systems.method: On-device deep-learning models for noise cancellation, background-voice cancellation, and dereverberation ('room echo removal'); ships as native SDKs (Windows/Mac/Linux/iOS/Android) plus a WASM SDK that runs entirely in-browser, processing audio locally without sending it to Krisp's servers for the core NC/BVC path. Krisp also ships a separate accent-conversion feature described as powered by 'a single adaptive model' — Krisp does not publicly state whether this shares a model family with the noise-cancellation model.
systems.availability: Consumer desktop and mobile app (Windows/Mac/iOS/Android) plus a licensable Voice SDK (native + Web/WASM) for Windows, Mac, Linux, Web, iOS, and Android, gated behind a sales-approved commercial licence (Early Stage / Enterprise developer tiers, apply via krisp.ai/developers), and a separate self-serve API with Python/JavaScript SDKs.
systems.best_for: Bolting proven per-call noise/echo cleanup onto an existing softphone, meeting app, or voice-agent pipeline without training your own model — the SDK is CPU-only and has a real in-browser WASM build, so it drops into a laptop-mic demo with no GPU and sub-20ms added latency, where commercial support and an SLA matter more than being able to inspect or fine-tune the model.
systems.watch: The SDK has no public price list and requires a sales-approved commercial licence — budget for a negotiation cycle, not a self-serve checkout, before it can ship in a product. The consumer app no longer offers a permanent free tier as of Aug 2026, only a 7-day trial.
systems.standout: A genuine in-browser WASM build (12 MB package, ~100 MB runtime memory) alongside native desktop/mobile SDKs, running entirely on-device with 'no server connectivity' per the vendor's own SDK docs — unusual among commercial vendors, and it means the same models work offline and keep audio off the network.
systems.quality_note: No PESQ/MOS scores published; Krisp's own methodology write-up describes testing via ITU-T P.835 (3QUEST: S-MOS/N-MOS/G-MOS), PESQ and POLQA but does not release the resulting numbers.
systems.latency_note: Krisp states sub-20ms audio-processing latency and 3-7% CPU usage for the real-time SDK path; SDK docs separately state ~1.5-2ms per-frame processing time on 10ms audio chunks for the native SDK, with the JS/WASM browser build reporting higher CPU usage than the native build (all vendor-reported, no independent measurement found).
systems.adoption: Vendor states '200M+ Devices worldwide' and that its RTC SDK (noise cancellation) handles 80B+ minutes of conversations MONTHLY, with cumulative processing of 'over 4T mins of voice conversations' and its separate VIVA SDK (voice-agent features) processing 1B+ minutes/month. All figures are self-reported company statistics, not independently audited.
systems.released: Company founded 2017; noise-cancellation app publicly launched and won ProductHunt's Audio & Video Product of the Year in 2018
systems.verification_note: On-device/CPU-only architecture, platform support, and the 200M+ devices figure are confirmed on Krisp's own SDK docs page; the privacy policy explicitly states NC/BVC audio 'does not leave the users' devices,' supporting the self-hostable/browser/cpu-capable facets. Pricing was re-checked live against krisp.ai/pricing/ as of Aug 2026: no permanent free tier exists today, only a 7-day trial. Cumulative/monthly minute figures and footprint/latency numbers are vendor-reported and not independently audited.

systems.name: WebRTC Audio Processing Module — Noise Suppression (NS)
systems.price_note: Free, open source — ships as a library inside libwebrtc; not sold or distributed as a standalone product.
systems.method: Classic per-band spectral-subtraction / Wiener-filter gain estimation driven by an adaptive noise-spectrum estimator (quantile noise estimator, Wiener filter, FFT-based band analysis) — pre-deep-learning digital signal processing, not a neural network.
systems.availability: C++ source inside the libwebrtc monorepo (modules/audio_processing/ns/); reachable directly by anyone building against libwebrtc, or indirectly via any WebRTC-based app (Chrome, most browser-based video calling, many VoIP SDKs) that leaves the built-in noise suppression enabled.
systems.best_for: The zero-integration-cost baseline you already have if you're building on WebRTC (Chrome, most browser calling stacks) and haven't disabled it — adequate for steady-state fan/hum-type noise, not for the harder cases a laptop mic actually produces.
systems.watch: This is spectral-subtraction/Wiener-filter DSP from the pre-neural-network era of noise suppression; on genuinely noisy or non-stationary sources it visibly underperforms RNNoise or DeepFilterNet, and there is no public roadmap from the WebRTC project to replace it with a neural model inside core libwebrtc.
systems.standout: Ships inside libwebrtc itself, so on a WebRTC-based stack it costs zero extra integration and runs everywhere WebRTC already runs (billions of endpoints via Chrome and WebRTC-based calling apps) rather than being an add-on you have to bring in separately.
systems.latency_note: Runs inside WebRTC's real-time audio processing pipeline (alongside the AEC and AGC stages), where hard real-time operation is a structural requirement of the APM design. Specific code-size ('a few kilobytes') and minimum-hardware ('decade-old phone') figures could not be corroborated in the WebRTC project's own documentation and are not repeated here.
systems.adoption: Ships by default inside libwebrtc, so it runs inside Chrome's WebRTC stack and any application built on it; no separate usage figures are published for the NS module in isolation.
systems.released: WebRTC was open-sourced by Google in 2011. The current NS module's earliest source-tree copyright header reads 2012; an exact ship date for this specific submodule (versus the broader audio processing pipeline) is not established from the sources reviewed.
systems.verification_note: License (BSD-3-Clause, confirmed against the repo's LICENSE file) and algorithm (quantile noise estimator, Wiener filter, FFT-based band analysis — confirmed via source file names/structure: quantile_noise_estimator.cc, wiener_filter.cc, ns_fft.cc) verified directly against the WebRTC source tree. The performance claims originally in latency_note and the precise NS-module release date were not found in WebRTC's own g3doc and are not independently verified.

systems.name: WebRTC AEC3
systems.licence: BSD-3-Clause (WebRTC project licence, with a separate royalty-free patent grant)
systems.method: Partitioned block frequency-domain adaptive filter (NLMS-style) for the linear echo path, plus a separate non-linear residual-echo suppressor stage; operates on 10 ms input frames processed internally in 64-sample (4 ms) blocks.
systems.availability: Source only, inside the full WebRTC source tree (webrtc.googlesource.com/src, mirrored on GitHub/Chromium); no small standalone package — build it via WebRTC's gn/ninja toolchain, or consume it by embedding libwebrtc / a Chromium-based runtime.
systems.best_for: Any product that already embeds Chromium or libwebrtc (browsers, Electron apps, native VoIP/video apps) and wants the exact echo canceller the browser itself runs, at zero licensing cost.
systems.watch: There's no lightweight 'AEC3-only' download — adopting it means either pulling in the whole WebRTC build (a substantial, Google-toolchain-specific build system) or using an extraction project like webrtc-audio-processing below, which does that packaging for you (Linux only).
systems.standout: The reference implementation most other consumer/browser echo cancellers get compared against — it's the AEC running in every Chrome tab, Google Meet call, and libwebrtc-based app already.
systems.quality_note: No PESQ/STOI/SI-SDR figures published by the WebRTC project itself. A third-party technical write-up (not Google's own docs) reports the linear-filter stage typically reaching 20-40 dB ERLE with about 1-2s convergence, with sub-10 dB ERLE indicating the filter failed to converge — cited here as a secondary source, not an independently verified benchmark.
systems.latency_note: Processes 10 ms frames in 64-sample (4 ms) blocks; the same third-party write-up states this comfortably fits a 4 ms real-time budget on mobile ARM CPUs. WebRTC's own header comments confirm the frame/block sizes but state no explicit latency target.
systems.adoption: Default echo canceller in Chrome/Chromium's WebRTC audio pipeline (the getUserMedia echoCancellation constraint) and in effectively every native app built on libwebrtc; also selectable as a backend in the PJSIP/PJMEDIA SIP stack — confirmed directly in PJSIP's own source as the PJMEDIA_HAS_WEBRTC_AEC3 compile-time flag (pjmedia/include/pjmedia/config.h) and the PJMEDIA_ECHO_WEBRTC_AEC3 runtime selector (pjmedia/include/pjmedia/echo.h), alongside the older PJMEDIA_HAS_WEBRTC_AEC / PJMEDIA_ECHO_WEBRTC for pre-AEC3 WebRTC AEC.
systems.released: ~2017 (added to the WebRTC codebase as the successor to the older AEC/AECM modules, per project history and code review records)
systems.verification_note: Source, licence, frame/block sizes, and adoption facts are confirmed from WebRTC's own source tree and PJSIP's own docs. The ERLE/convergence quality figures and the 4 ms latency-budget claim trace to a third-party technical explainer, not Google's own documentation, and no independent benchmark study was found.

systems.name: SpeexDSP Echo Canceller
systems.licence: BSD-3-Clause (Xiph.Org Foundation, with additional historical copyright holders including Jean-Marc Valin)
systems.method: Multi-delay block frequency-domain adaptive filter (MDF, per J.S. Soo & K.K. Pang, 1990), using the Alternatively Updated MDF (AUMDF) variant — a plain C adaptive-filter algorithm, no neural network involved. Per the library's own source comments (mdf.c), there is no explicit double-talk detector; double-talk robustness instead comes from a continuously variable learning rate (per Valin, "On Adjusting the Learning Rate in Frequency-Domain Echo Cancellation With Double-Talk"), not a discrete detection step.
systems.availability: Source (plain C library) at gitlab.xiph.org/xiph/speexdsp, mirrored on GitHub; packaged as libspeexdsp in essentially every major Linux distro plus Homebrew, and wrapped by third-party bindings (e.g. Python) for other languages.
systems.best_for: Lightweight, dependency-free echo cancellation for embedded/IoT devices or any C/C++ project (SIP stacks, telephony middleware) that wants a small adaptive-filter AEC without pulling in the full WebRTC build toolchain.
systems.watch: Active development happens on gitlab.xiph.org, not the GitHub mirror shown in most search results. It is easy to conflate SpeexDSP (the still-used processing/AEC library) with the separate Speex audio codec, which Xiph has deprecated in favour of Opus — the codec's deprecation does not apply to the DSP/AEC library.
systems.standout: The smallest, most portable footprint of any option here — a dependency-free C library still used as a compile-time AEC backend in mainstream open-source SIP stacks.
systems.quality_note: No PESQ/STOI/SI-SDR or ERLE figures were found published by Xiph or in an independent study for this specific echo-canceller module — none is cited here.
systems.latency_note: Real-time, frame-based processing intended for telephony use (the Speex API operates on fixed-size frames); no formal real-time-factor or end-to-end latency figure is published by Xiph.
systems.adoption: Selectable as a compile-time AEC backend (PJMEDIA_ECHO_SPEEX, enabled by default via PJMEDIA_HAS_SPEEX_AEC) in the PJSIP/PJMEDIA SIP stack, alongside the WebRTC AEC/AEC3 backends, per PJSIP's own source (pjmedia/include/pjmedia/echo.h, config.h).
systems.verification_note: Licence and copyright holders confirmed against the repository's COPYING file (BSD-3-Clause style; Xiph.Org Foundation, Jean-Marc Valin, Analog Devices Inc., CSIRO, David Rowe, and others). The MDF / Soo & Pang (1990) citation and AUMDF variant are confirmed from mdf.c's own header comments — but that same source explicitly states "there is no explicit double-talk detection," which contradicted this row's original method description and has been corrected. PJSIP's role as a selectable (in fact default-on) AEC backend is confirmed from PJMEDIA source, correcting the macro name from PJMEDIA_EC_SPEEX to PJMEDIA_ECHO_SPEEX. No PESQ/STOI/SI-SDR/ERLE quality figures were found published by Xiph or in an independent study; none are claimed.

systems.name: webrtc-audio-processing (PulseAudio / PipeWire)
systems.method: Repackages Google's AudioProcessing module — the same AEC3 algorithm described in the WebRTC AEC3 row above — as a standalone, Meson-built C++ library decoupled from the full WebRTC/Chromium build, for easy distro packaging.
systems.availability: Source (Meson build) at gitlab.freedesktop.org/pulseaudio/webrtc-audio-processing; packaged by essentially every major Linux distro as libwebrtc-audio-processing and consumed automatically by PulseAudio's module-echo-cancel and by PipeWire's echo-cancel module.
systems.best_for: Linux desktop or server users who want echo cancellation applied system-wide — to any application's microphone stream, not just one that embeds an AEC library itself — with zero changes to the application.
systems.watch: It only repackages Google's algorithm for easier Linux packaging; it adds no processing of its own, so quality and bugs are ultimately bounded by upstream AEC3. Major version bumps (e.g. the 1.x to 2.x jump tracking newer WebRTC milestones) have broken API compatibility and required PulseAudio/PipeWire config or build updates.
systems.standout: The only option on this list that fixes echo for a whole machine at once rather than one app — PipeWire and PulseAudio apply it transparently to any application's mic input.
systems.quality_note: Inherits whatever quality applies to the upstream AEC3 algorithm it packages (see the WebRTC AEC3 row) — no separate accuracy figures were found for this packaging layer specifically.
systems.latency_note: Shares AEC3's underlying 10 ms frame / 64-sample block processing; no separate latency figure is published for the repackaged library itself.
systems.adoption: PipeWire's own documentation lists aec/libspa-aec-webrtc — built on this library — as the sole supported echo-cancellation backend for its echo-cancel module (the default when no backend is explicitly configured), and PulseAudio's module-echo-cancel also uses it as its "webrtc" aec_method. This is the default backend WHEN echo cancellation is enabled, not evidence that echo cancellation runs by default: neither PulseAudio nor PipeWire loads its echo-cancel module out of the box on mainstream distros — a user or distro integrator must explicitly configure it — so "default system-wide AEC on most Linux desktops" overstates actual deployment and was dropped.
systems.verification_note: PipeWire's own docs confirm it as the (only) supported echo-cancel backend, and the BSD licence/packaging facts come from the project's own repo and mirrors. Underlying quality claims are inherited from — and only as verified as — the upstream AEC3 row.

systems.name: Agora AI Noise Suppression
systems.licence: Proprietary — usage-based commercial add-on to the Agora RTC SDK
systems.price_note: $0.59 per 1,000 processed minutes, with the first 10,000 minutes/month free; Agora offers custom volume discounts for high-usage accounts (no published minutes threshold); a separate $500/month Cloud Proxy base fee applies only if firewall traversal is also used
systems.method: Deep-learning denoising + dereverberation delivered as a pluggable extension inside the Agora RTC SDK — a WASM extension on Web, native plugins (e.g. an iOS xcframework) on mobile/desktop — running client-side on the caller's own device inside the existing RTC audio pipeline; billed per processed minute separately from core RTC.
systems.availability: Self-serve via the Agora Console/SDK on Web, Android, iOS, macOS, Windows, Electron, Flutter, React Native and Unity; requires Agora's core RTC SDK (v4.15.0+ on Web) as the base
systems.best_for: Real-time voice/video apps already built on Agora's RTC SDK for transport that want to bolt on per-minute-metered noise/reverb cleanup rather than adopt a whole separate audio-processing stack.
systems.watch: Agora's own docs describe this add-on as noise suppression + dereverberation only, but the marketing product page separately claims it 'removes reverberation and echoing' — acoustic/line echo cancellation for the call itself is a distinct, built-in RTC feature, not part of what this add-on bills for.
systems.standout: Priced and metered per processed minute rather than per seat, so cost scales directly with call volume, and it plugs straight into an RTC SDK many voice-agent stacks already use for transport.
systems.quality_note: No PESQ/MOS figures published; the product page claims suppression of '100+ types of background noise' without citing a test set or score.
systems.latency_note: Docs mention an 'Aggressive mode with low latency' but do not publish a millisecond figure.
systems.verification_note: Pricing, feature scope, and platform support are all from agora.io's own pricing/product pages and docs.agora.io implementation guides; no independent quality benchmark was found.

systems.name: SoliCall Pro / Connect
systems.licence: Proprietary — per-seat commercial licence (Pro/Connect desktop apps) plus separately-licensed OEM SDKs (Mobile & Client SDK, Server SDK)
systems.price_note: No public price list on solicall.com; per-seat pricing is quote-based (third-party marketplaces report roughly $30-50/seat, unverified — not stated by SoliCall directly)
systems.method: Proprietary bi-directional noise-cancellation and echo-cancellation DSP applied client-side (SoliCall Pro desktop app, Windows) or server/gateway-side (SoliCall Connect 'Noise Firewall', PBXMate, Server SDK), working across existing phone/VoIP/PBX systems rather than a specific RTC engine; runs CPU-only with no GPU required.
systems.availability: Commercial Windows desktop app for individual users; separately-licensed server-side/call-center and OEM SDK products (Mobile & Client SDK, Server SDK) for integrators
systems.best_for: Call centers and telephony/PBX environments needing noise and echo cleanup bolted onto an existing, non-WebRTC phone system without replacing the softphone stack.
systems.watch: No public pricing or hardware spec sheet is published — 'minimal CPU, no GPU' and 'minimal memory' are stated on the marketing site without numbers, and per-seat cost must be requested directly from sales.
systems.standout: Explicitly bi-directional and 'Noise Firewall'-branded for shared call-center floors, suppressing cross-talk from neighboring agents on both legs of a call — a scenario most single-stream noise-suppression SDKs don't target.
systems.quality_note: No PESQ/MOS figures or independent benchmark found; claims are qualitative only ('advanced', 'patented').
systems.adoption: Vendor states 'million calls filtered per day' (homepage: 'million calls filtered per day'; About page: 'improves the audio quality of 21 million calls every day') with years-in-operation that vary by page (homepage 'track record' cites 19 years; About page cites 20 years). Site displays an additional 'countries served' stat counter but no number was resolvable from the static page content, so it is omitted rather than stated as sourced. Unverified vendor claims; no independent figures found.
systems.verification_note: All facts sourced from solicall.com's own homepage and products page; no independent review, benchmark, or third-party audit was found, and the company's self-reported years-in-operation figure is inconsistent across its own pages.

gaps: Krisp was independently discovered twice, once under `noise-suppression` and once under `commercial-suite` -- merged into a single `commercial-suite` row since it is fundamentally a commercial product bundling multiple audio-processing capabilities (noise cancellation, background-voice cancellation, dereverberation, accent conversion), not a single-purpose noise-suppression tool.

NVIDIA's Maxine Audio Effects SDK was independently discovered three times under three different names and categories (`noise-suppression`, `echo-cancellation`, `commercial-suite`) -- the same product family across several NVIDIA doc-page generations. Merged into a single `commercial-suite` row for the same reason as Krisp: one commercial SDK bundling noise removal, AEC, and dereverberation, not three separate single-purpose tools. A reader filtering specifically for `echo-cancellation` or `noise-suppression` alone will not see this row -- the same trade-off already made for Krisp.

`WebRTC AEC3` (`echo-cancellation`) and `webrtc-audio-processing` (`echo-cancellation`) are the same underlying Google libwebrtc echo-cancellation algorithm, differing only in packaging -- AEC3 as it ships inside the full libwebrtc source tree/build system, vs. a standalone Linux extraction project that packages the same algorithm separately for non-Chromium consumers (PulseAudio/PipeWire). Deliberately kept as two rows rather than merged: the packaging difference is a real, reader-facing choice (pulling in the whole WebRTC gn/ninja build vs. a small standalone Linux library), unlike the Resemblyzer/WeSpeaker/ECAPA-TDNN/Krisp/Maxine cases above where the duplication was purely an artifact of the research pass discovering one system under two category labels.
